nature-econ-626.title: Anti-rival goods: better the more people use them
nature-econ-626.text: Some goods get better the more people use them. Any natural language is one: it is more useful the more people speak it. Such a good is anti-rival. Steven Weber introduced the idea in 2004, noting that free and open-source software improves for everyone as more people use it. Efforts against climate change are perversely anti-rival, because a free-riding country still gains from others' efforts.

nature-econ-608.title: The comedy of the commons: the more the merrier
nature-econ-608.text: Not every commons ends in tragedy. In a 1986 article the legal scholar Carol M. Rose described the opposite case, the comedy of the commons. Here a shared resource becomes more valuable to each user the more people use it: 'the more the merrier'. Her examples were commerce and group recreation. Rose argued that such resources are more likely to suffer from too little investment than from overuse.

nature-econ-666.title: Social traps: short-term gain, long-term loss
nature-econ-666.text: Taking the car instead of public transport buys comfort now and more greenhouse gas emissions later. That is a social trap: people act for short-term personal gain in a way that, in the long run, leaves the whole group worse off. John Platt introduced the term in a 1973 paper, applying behavioral psychology to Hardin's tragedy of the commons. Social traps are blamed for overfishing, overgrazing in the Sahel, rainforest destruction and, above all, climate change. Platt proposed ways out: rewards for green behavior, and penalties such as pollution taxes.

nature-econ-624.title: Locke's labor theory of property: mixing work with nature
nature-econ-624.text: Mix your labor with something no one owns, and the result becomes yours. That is John Locke's labor theory of property, set out in his Second Treatise of Government (1689). It starts from the claim that each person owns their own self. There is a condition: 'enough and as good' must be left for others, a requirement called the Lockean proviso. Libertarians cite the tragedy of the commons as what happens when governments forbid people to claim resources in the Lockean way.

nature-econ-650.title: Georgism and the environment: pollution as a taking from the commons
nature-econ-650.text: To a Georgist, pollution is a taking from the commons, so its value should be captured for the public through taxes or quotas. Henry George partly inspired early conservation efforts in the Progressive Era, explored in {{ref:nature-hist-014}}. Georgists and ecological economists both favor market-based limits on pollution, but Georgists insist the income should not go to polluters. Their 'cap and share' would auction temporary pollution permits and give the proceeds to the public, instead of handing permits free to polluters. Some ecological economists also back a tax on land values, to free unused land for nature and curb urban sprawl.

nature-econ-662.title: The Diamond–Mirrlees theorem: keep production efficient
nature-econ-662.text: Even a government that cannot use lump-sum taxes should not waste resources in production. That was the 1971 result of Peter Diamond and James Mirrlees: production efficiency stays desirable without lump-sum taxes. It is credited with modernizing Ramsey's analysis of taxation by considering how income is distributed together with raising revenue. Stiglitz and Dasgupta (1971) argued it is not robust if some tax tools cannot be used.

nature-econ-689.title: The Nash bargaining solution: splitting the gains from agreement
nature-econ-689.text: Two parties can gain by agreeing, but how should they split the gains? John Nash (1950) defined a bargaining problem as the set of possible agreements plus what each gets if talks fail, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-688}}. His solution picks the agreement that maximizes the product of each player's gain over that fallback, called the Nash product. Like other bargaining solutions, it is built from axioms such as efficiency, symmetry and independence of irrelevant alternatives. It handles only the simplest structure, though, and does not show how efficient outcomes are reached over time.

nature-econ-654.title: The Lindahl tax: each pays what the good is worth to them
nature-econ-654.text: Sarah and Tom want a park that costs $15 per acre. At the 60th acre, Sarah would pay $5 and Tom $10 for one more: together, exactly $15. So they build 60 acres, and each pays that share per acre. That is a Lindahl tax, proposed by the Swedish economist Erik Lindahl in 1919 under the influence of his teacher Knut Wicksell. Each person pays according to their own marginal benefit, so everyone is better off and may agree. In theory it provides public goods efficiently. In practice it needs each person's demand, which people may hide, may not know, and government may struggle to add up.

nature-econ-628.title: Club theory: how big should a club be
nature-econ-628.text: How big should a club be, and how should its members share the costs? James M. Buchanan founded club theory in 1965 to answer those questions. He saw a gap between purely private and purely public goods: excludable goods shared by more people than a private good but fewer than a public one. Each new member lowers the cost per head but adds congestion, so there is an optimal size. Cornes and Sandler's conditions lead to two-part pricing, a fixed membership fee plus a charge per use. Olson and Zeckhauser (1967) applied the theory to cost-sharing in NATO, asking whether some members were free riding.

nature-econ-667.title: Social dilemmas: when selfishness pays but cooperation pays more
nature-econ-667.text: Each person does better by acting selfishly, whatever the others do. Yet everyone would do best if all cooperated. That is a social dilemma. Robyn Dawes coined the term a few years after Platt, to cover both social traps and dilemmas over shared resources. There are three main kinds: large-scale dilemmas, commons or resource dilemmas, and public goods dilemmas. Uncertainty about others' actions or about the resource discourages cooperation, but a trustworthy leader who manages the resource fairly can restore it.

nature-econ-607.title: The commons dilemma: self-interest against the group
nature-econ-607.text: A commons dilemma is a social dilemma in which people's short-term selfish interests clash with the long-term interests of the group and the common good. Researchers study, in the laboratory and the field, when groups under- or over-harvest common resources. Order matters: when people harvest in a fixed order, those who go first take more. So does being watched. People take less from a common pool when others can see them than when they act anonymously. Selective punishments for overuse, such as installing water and electricity meters in houses, can encourage conservation.

nature-econ-664.title: Res communis: things that belong to everyone
nature-econ-664.text: Roman law held that some things belong to all humankind: air, running water, the sea and its shores. This idea, res communis, was codified in the Institutes of Justinian in the 6th century, long before modern ideas of the commons. It differs from res publica, public property managed by government, because common things are for everyone to use and enjoy. In laws protecting the environment, it means the state is trustee of shared natural resources and cannot sell them into private hands. Fish and mammals on the high seas are examples, and the rules for Antarctica and for space law were built on it.

nature-econ-663.title: The public trust doctrine: resources the state holds for all
nature-econ-663.text: The shore between high and low tide can stay open to the public, whoever owns the land beside it. That is the public trust doctrine: the state holds certain resources in trust for public use. It goes back to Roman law. It passed into English law and then US common law, covering tidal and navigable waters and the minerals and animals in them. It has been used to claim oil under tidal lands for the public and to stop private ownership of fish stocks and shellfish beds.

nature-econ-645.title: The bundle of rights: ownership as a set of sticks
nature-econ-645.text: Owning land is less like holding one thing than holding a bundle of sticks. Each stick is a separate right that can be split off, given to someone else and later put back. The idea began with Wesley Newcomb Hohfeld in 1913, though he never used the phrase. The five traditional rights are possession, control, exclusion, enjoyment, meaning use including resource extraction, and disposition, or transfer. A tenant may live on land while someone else owns the minerals or water beneath it. Governments keep rights such as environmental regulation, land-use rules and eminent domain, and third parties may hold others, such as {{ref:nature-mkt-126}}.

nature-econ-669.title: Usufruct: the right to use without owning
nature-econ-669.text: 'Earth belongs in usufruct to the living,' Thomas Jefferson wrote in 1789: each generation may use it but must not impoverish it. Usufruct is the right to use someone else's property, often land, and take its fruits or profits, without owning or damaging it. It combines usus, the right to use, and fructus, the right to profit; full ownership adds abusus, the right to sell or destroy. In the western United States, rights to water are usufruct rights, lost if not put to full beneficial use.

nature-econ-655.title: Preference revelation: getting honest answers about public goods
nature-econ-655.text: How much would you pay for a public good you can enjoy for free? Honest answers are hard to get, and there is no market to make people show what the good is worth. That is the problem of preference revelation. Only individuals know their own benefit, and they have a reason to understate it, a form of free riding. Without full knowledge of preferences, government planners are likely to supply too much or too little. Mechanisms such as {{ref:nature-econ-637}} aim to draw out true values, but none has fully solved the problem, and asking a large population is costly in money and time.

nature-econ-637.title: The Vickrey-Clarke-Groves mechanism: making honesty pay
nature-econ-637.text: Ask people what a public good is worth to them, and they have reason to understate it. The Vickrey-Clarke-Groves mechanism, one of the best-studied procedures for deciding how much of a public good to fund and who pays, tries to make honesty pay. Each participant is paid the total value of everyone else, so its own welfare matches society's and telling the truth is its best strategy. Most work uses the Clarke pivot rule, which makes sure everyone pays in and no one is worse off for taking part. It needs a great deal of information from each user, which has helped keep it out of practice.

nature-econ-638.title: Quadratic funding: small gifts, big matching
nature-econ-638.text: Quadratic funding is a recent way to fund public goods, developed by Buterin, Hitzig and Weyl from quadratic voting. Each contributor gives a single amount, and a subsidy tops up the total. Like the VCG mechanism it needs a subsidy, so there is always a deficit the designer must cover. It is also vulnerable to collusion between contributors and to fake identities, known as sybil attacks.

nature-econ-648.title: The Environmental Goods Agreement: trade talks that collapsed
nature-econ-648.text: In 2015, 18 members of {{ref:nature-pol-007}} began talks to cut tariffs on goods used to protect the environment. In trade usage, 'environmental goods' means such products: renewable energy technology and pollution control systems, for example. The talks aimed to spread cleaner technologies for air pollution control, waste treatment, renewable energy, monitoring and energy efficiency. They collapsed in 2016.

nature-econ-670.title: Impure public goods: partly shared, partly not
nature-econ-670.text: Most goods called public are not purely so. An impure public good is non-rival and non-excludable only partly, or only some of the time. Since pure public goods are rare, most public goods are impure in practice. Public property is sometimes treated as a public good, usually an impure one. Some parts of cybersecurity, such as sharing threat information and protecting critical infrastructure and election integrity, behave this way.

nature-econ-668.title: The tragedy of the anticommons: too many owners, too little use
nature-econ-668.text: In post-communist Eastern European cities, Michael Heller noticed empty shops. Too many parties held rights over each space. In a 1998 article he named this the tragedy of the anticommons. When a resource has many owners who can each block its use, it ends up underused. Early aviation patents held by the Wright brothers and Glenn Curtiss blocked each other until the government created a patent pool in World War I. Remedies include eminent domain and patent pools. Heller and Eisenberg argue biological patents create an anticommons; others, citing surveys of scientists, disagree.

reviews.public-goods-commons-and-property: Two questions, whether people can be kept out and whether use leaves less for others, sort goods into private goods, club goods, common-pool resources and public goods, and each type brings its own trouble. Public goods invite free riding, so they tend to be under-supplied unless governments, nonprofits, assurance contracts or Lindahl taxes step in, while common-pool resources invite the overuse Hardin called the tragedy of the commons. Property rights offer one answer, and if transaction costs are low enough the Coase theorem says bargaining can fix a harm whoever holds the rights, though holdouts, free riders and anger often block the deal. Ostrom showed another way, in which communities write, watch and enforce their own rules for shared resources. Old legal ideas such as res communis, the public trust doctrine and usufruct carry the same question into law: who may use nature, and on what terms.
